think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 39-year-old Nigerian immigrant with sickle cell disease presents with a massive, painless, non-erythematous, 16-cm fluctuant mass on her left flank that grew over two years, accompanied by lower back pain radiating to the left lower quadrant. The presentation is devoid of acute constitutional signs (fever, chills, night sweats, leukocytosis). The clinical dilemma is distinguishing a tuberculous cold abscess with Pott's disease originating from L4-L5 diskitis/osteomyelitis from pyogenic spondylodiscitis (such as Salmonella or Staphylococcus in a patient with hemoglobinopathy), benign soft-tissue tumor (cystic hygroma, hematoma), or retroperitoneal neoplasm.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following physical examination of the fluctuant flank mass, baseline lab tests (showing sickle cell anemia, normal WBC, sterile routine blood cultures), and cross-sectional abdominal/lumbar MRI demonstrating L4-L5 diskitis/osteomyelitis with contiguous retroperitoneal and subcutaneous cold abscess, immediately prior to ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration and mycobacterial cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pyogenic diskitis and osteomyelitis (especially Salmonella osteomyelitis or S. aureus in sickle cell disease; typically presents with acute severe localized spinal tenderness, high fever, elevated WBC, and positive blood/routine bacterial cultures, which were absent here); soft-tissue cystic neoplasm / hematoma (painless expanding mass in a patient with hemoglobinopathy, ruled out by MRI demonstrating bony destruction of L4-L5 and viscous purulent fluid on aspiration); spinal tuberculosis / Pott's disease with cold abscess (chronic indolent diskitis, absence of acute inflammation, extensive retroperitoneal gravitation abscess, confirmed by positive Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture from drained viscous fluid).
case_prompt: A 39-year-old Nigerian woman with a history of sickle cell disease presents to the hospital with a chief complaint of a progressively enlarging mass on her left flank over the past 2 years. She initially noted the swelling as a 1-cm soft, painless nodule that gradually enlarged to approximately 10 cm. She reports no warmth, erythema, tenderness, or drainage from the site. Six months prior to presentation, she developed dull midline lower back pain radiating laterally to the left lower quadrant, which fluctuates in severity and worsens with spinal flexion. She reports no fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, cough, hemoptysis, or dyspnea, and has no bowel, bladder, or lower extremity neurological symptoms. She immigrated from Nigeria to the United States 1 year ago and received the BCG vaccine in childhood. Physical examination reveals a well-appearing, afebrile woman (temperature 98.8°F, blood pressure 118/60 mmHg, heart rate 66 beats per minute). She has scleral icterus and multiple nontender, mobile cervical lymph nodes, the largest measuring 2 cm in the right anterior cervical chain. Examination of the back reveals a 10 cm × 16 cm well-demarcated, fluctuant, non-tender mass over the left flank without erythema or local warmth; spinal range of motion is intact with no focal bony spinal tenderness. Laboratory studies reveal hemoglobin of 94 g/L, MCV 92.5 fL, leukocyte count 7.4 × 10³/µL, platelet count 317 × 10³/µL, total bilirubin 148.8 µmol/L (indirect bilirubin 131.7 µmol/L), LDH 525 U/L, and ESR 28 mm/hr. Rapid HIV screening is negative, and blood cultures drawn on admission remain sterile at 48 hours. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine demonstrate diskitis and osteomyelitis at L4–L5 with an expansile disc abscess extending into the ventral epidural space, neural foramina, and contiguous large paraspinal and left retroperitoneal abscesses extending into the left lower back and flank subcutaneous tissue.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic bacterial spondylodiscitis and retroperitoneal abscess (e.g., Salmonella or Staphylococcus aureus)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered high on the differential because patients with sickle cell disease are predisposed to bone infarcts and pyogenic osteomyelitis/bacteremia from Salmonella and Staphylococcus aureus. However, pyogenic spondylodiscitis typically presents acutely with high fevers, severe spinal tenderness, leukocytosis, and bacteremia, whereas this patient had an indolent 2-year afebrile course, normal WBC, negative routine blood cultures, and sterile initial Gram stains.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Blood cultures drawn at initial evaluation remained sterile after 48 hours.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Soft tissue neoplasm or chronic organized hematoma
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the patient's hemoglobinopathy and a slowly growing, painless, non-erythematous fluctuant flank mass over several years without systemic B symptoms. Ruled out by MRI showing destructive L4-L5 diskitis and osteomyelitis with contiguous retroperitoneal fluid tracking, and thick viscous purulent fluid on aspiration.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed diskitis/osteomyelitis at the L4-L5 level with adjacent paraspinal and left retroperitoneal abscesses extending to the left lower back/flank subcutaneous tissue and into the epidural space.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Aspiration of the viscous flank mass yielded purulent fluid with 82% neutrophils, and subsequent mycobacterial cultures confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis from the drained abscess, confirming spinal tuberculosis with an extensive gravitating cold abscess.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Four weeks from presentation, cultures from drained abscess revealed Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly from PMC5187466_01 following Stanford MedCaseReasoning guidelines. The presentation maintains the diagnostic challenge of an afebrile cold abscess with diskitis/osteomyelitis in a patient with hemoglobinopathy.
